commit.message:
peer+server: use the RBF close flow for aux channels that support it

Aux channels were excluded from the RBF coop close flow outright, as the
state machine didn't drive the aux closer hooks. Now that it does,
relax the exclusion: an aux channel uses the RBF flow if the aux closer
reports support for the channel, which lets the aux closer negotiate
that with its peer, since the RBF feature bits alone are peer level.
Without such support the channel keeps using the legacy closer.

Wire the aux closer, the channel view and the delivery address internal
key lookup into the RBF closer's environment, and report the close
outputs of the confirmed transaction in the final close update, like
the legacy closer does.

With that, the RBF coop close protocol is also auto-enabled when
taproot overlay channels are enabled, as it already is for plain
taproot channels.

commit.message:
chancloser: drive the aux closer hooks from the RBF close state machine

The RBF coop close state machine didn't invoke any of the aux closer
hooks: the shutdown it sent carried no aux custom records, and the close
transactions it negotiated carried no aux outputs. For a taproot asset
channel that means the funding output, which anchors the asset
commitment, is spent by a transaction that doesn't re-commit the assets.

Thread the hooks through the state machine the same way the legacy
closer does:

  * The Environment gains an optional AuxCloser, a ChanInfo view of the
    channel (initiator, commit fee, blobs, dust limits) and a lookup for
    the internal key of our delivery address.

  * When we send shutdown, the aux closer's custom records are included
    in the message. The records of both parties are carried through
    ShutdownPending, ChannelFlushing and into the close terms.

  * The fee estimates account for the fee-independent shape of the aux
    outputs, and the concrete outputs are validated against that shape
    before we sign.

  * Every signing round asks the aux closer for the extra outputs, with
    the fee of that round and the party paying it. The closer pays in
    the RBF flow, so the local flow passes Local and the remote flow
    passes Remote. The outputs we signed for in our offer are reused
    when the remote party's signature completes it, so the exact same
    transaction is completed.

  * We only act as the closer if our own output stays above dust after
    paying the fee, as the channel omits a dust output and with it the
    aux output of our party, which carries the assets. In that case the
    remote party needs to be the closer.

  * A remote party can't switch its delivery script through
    closing_complete once aux records were exchanged, as the records are
    bound to the script they were sent with. A new shutdown is required
    for that.

  * The terminal state reports the close outputs and aux outputs of
    whichever negotiated transaction confirmed, so the caller can be
    told about them.

commit.message:
contractcourt: hand the close fee to the aux closer on finalize

The aux closer needs the fee of the confirmed close transaction for the
transfer it records. With the RBF close flow the fee isn't known when the
aux outputs are created, so the chain watcher derives it from the
confirmed transaction and the channel capacity.

commit.message:
lnwallet: extend aux closer interface for the RBF close flow

Add a FeePayer field to AuxCloseDesc, so an aux closer can be told who
pays the close fee. The legacy negotiation always has the channel
initiator pay, which is what a None value means. The RBF flow has the
party that proposes a close transaction pay its fee, so it sets the
field explicitly.

Also add SupportsRbfClose to the AuxChanCloser interface. The RBF coop
close feature bits are negotiated at the peer level, but an aux channel
can only use the RBF flow if the aux closers on both sides drive their
hooks from within it. This lets the aux closer make that call per
channel, based on whatever it negotiated with the peer.

commit.message:
chancloser: derive the co-op close fee from the vsize

Relay policy is enforced on the virtual size of a transaction, which
rounds its weight up to whole vbytes. The co-op close fee was derived
from the raw weight estimate instead, so at the relay floor it could
fall a satoshi short: a taproot close with two P2TR outputs is estimated
at 615 weight units, which is 154 vbytes, but 615 weight units at
1 sat/vbyte is 153 sats, and the mempool rejects the transaction.

The legacy closer masked this by estimating with the (larger) multisig
witness regardless of the channel type, while the RBF closer uses the
actual channel type and hit the floor. Compute the fee from the rounded
up vsize instead.

commit.message:
contractcourt: CPFP the second-level HTLC anchor through the sweeper

The pre-signed second-level HTLC tx cannot be RBF'd under SigHashDefault
(the peer's signature commits to the full tx), so CPFP via the anchor at
output index 1 is its only fee-bumping path. Build the anchor input and
pass it, with its budget, in the PublishPreSignedTx request, so the
sweeper CPFPs the parent as soon as it is in the mempool.

The anchor input carries a key-path sign descriptor and the parent tx
info the sweeper needs for package fee-rate calculation: the exact
baked-in parent fee (spent commitment output value minus the parent's
outputs) and the parent weight. The fee budget for the child is derived
from the value under protection (the second-level HTLC output) via the
same sweeper.budget.anchorcpfp(ratio) configuration used for commitment
anchor CPFP, plus the anchor value itself. The child is funded from
wallet inputs, so the budget can and usually must exceed the anchor's
own 330 sats. The deadline is the incoming HTLC's expiry on the timeout
path (matching the other timeout-path sweeps) and the HTLC's own expiry
on the success path.

The anchor is keyed to the broadcaster's to-local delay key, which is
derived directly from the second-level output's sweep sign descriptor
(delay base point + single tweak), keeping this path self-contained. No
anchor is attached when the parent tx has fewer than two outputs, i.e.
the channel did not use DeterministicHTLCs, or when the descriptor
lacks the key material; the parent then still publishes at its
baked-in floor fee.

sweep+contractcourt: publish pre-signed second-level HTLCs via the sweeper

When a second-level HTLC transaction was signed with SigHashDefault, the
peer's signature commits to the entire transaction: the sweeper's usual
flow of rebuilding the tx with extra fee inputs or batched outputs would
invalidate it. Such a transaction has to be published verbatim, and a
pre-signed timeout tx carries an absolute locktime, so it is only final
once the chain reaches that height and has to be retried on later
blocks after a "non final" or transient mempool rejection.

Rather than growing a second publication engine in contractcourt, hand
the whole lifecycle to the sweeper. UtxoSweeper gains
PublishPreSignedTx: the caller supplies the exact transaction, the
outputs it spends, an optional CPFP anchor input with its budget, and a
deadline, and the sweeper owns everything from there inside its
existing block-driven event loop: it watches the spent outputs, gates
publication on the locktime, re-broadcasts on every block until the
wallet accepts the tx, registers the anchor with its regular input
machinery once the parent is in the mempool, and reports a single final
outcome on the returned channel.

The lifecycle only ends on chain evidence. The sweeper registers a
spend notification for every input of the tx before it publishes
anything: the tx itself as the spender means it confirmed and only the
anchor is left to sweep, any other spender means it can never confirm
(ErrPreSignedTxConflict). Until then every step is retried on every
block: a rejected publication, including one the wallet reports as a
double spend, since the backend maps a missing input to the same error
and a commitment that is gone after a re-org comes back; a failed
anchor registration, which happens inline in the collector via
handleNewInput so that a nil error is a real acknowledgement; and an
anchor sweep that failed, most commonly because the parent left the
mempool (evicted or replaced) and nobody else re-broadcasts it, in which
case the lifecycle goes back to publishing the parent. The deadline
only drives the fee rate of the anchor child. It does not bound the
retries: the output the tx claims stays claimable past it, so giving up
there would abandon a valid claim over a transient error.

The anchor is registered with input batching disabled: it spends an
unconfirmed parent, and a parent that goes missing must only ever fail
the anchor's own sweep tx. Our child confirming, or a third party
spending the anchor, concludes the lifecycle, both imply the parent
confirmed.

Duplicate requests attach as additional listeners, shutdown releases
pending callers with ErrSweeperShuttingDown, and nothing is persisted:
like regular inputs, a resolver re-submits after a restart, at which
point an already-published tx is a no-op broadcast. The parent is
always published on its own. Submitting it together with its anchor
child as a package only works on bitcoind today, so that is left for
when btcd and neutrino support 1P1C relay, and can then be added inside
this one API without touching the resolvers.

On the contractcourt side the timeout and success resolvers detect the
SigHashDefault case through isSecondLevelSigHashDefault, which also
requires the channel type to carry a tapscript root: SigHashDefault is
the zero value of SigHashType, so without the explicit channel-type
check any channel that never populates SignDetails.SigHashType would
false-positively match. Only aux/custom (taproot asset) channels carry
a tapscript root, so non-custom channels provably keep using the sweeper
flow. The resolvers build the request, with the commitment HTLC output
as the spent output and the broadcast height as the height hint, and
hand it over; a tracked goroutine logs the eventual outcome. A
synchronous hand-off failure clears the resolver's launched flag so the
next Launch can retry instead of no-op'ing until restart.

lnwallet: add CPFP anchor to second-level HTLCs under SigHashDefault

When DeterministicHTLCs is negotiated (SigHashDefault second-level
HTLCs), the peer's signature commits to the entire transaction, so the
sweeper can neither add fee inputs nor RBF the pre-signed tx. Instead of
baking a large fixed fee into the transaction, give it a minimal
baked-in fee plus a CPFP anchor:

- The pre-signed second-level HTLC tx gets a second output: a taproot
  anchor (AnchorSize sats, keyed to the broadcaster's delay key) that
  the local party can sweep to CPFP-bump the package fee rate.
- The baked-in fee is 1.1x the relay floor over the tx weight (including
  the anchor output), which is enough for the pre-signed tx to clear
  min-relay on its own. It deliberately does not track the negotiated
  commitment fee rate: the whole on-chain BTC value of an aux-channel
  HTLC is a small fixed budget that already pays this fee, funds the
  anchor, and must still leave a second-level output that is non-dust
  AND able to fund the third-level sweep claiming it. At a realistic
  commitment fee rate the fee alone exceeds that budget, and capping it
  at what keeps the output non-dust leaves the output unable to pay for
  its own sweep, stranding the asset value it carries. Adapting to the
  fee market is the CPFP child's job. Where a mempool minimum sits above
  the parent's own rate, a separately published child cannot rescue a
  parent the mempool never accepted. That takes submitting both as a
  package, which only bitcoind supports today and is left for later.
- HtlcIsDust and the second-level fee/output-amount calculations are
  threaded with the sigHashDefault flag so dust decisions and the HTLC
  output value account for both the baked-in fee and the AnchorSize
  reduction. The flag is that of the commitment in question: the
  type its signer decided for a new commitment, the type recorded in
  its blob for one restored from disk, closed on chain or revoked.
- The sweep sign descriptor for the second-level output is reduced by
  AnchorSize accordingly, so the sweeper signs for the correct value.

Only aux/custom (taproot asset) channels can negotiate SigHashDefault
(see ResolveHtlcSigHashType); all other channel types keep their
existing fee and transaction form.

lnwallet+contractcourt: gate HTLC sighash on negotiated feature bit

Introduce a feature-bit negotiation approach for choosing the sighash
type of second-level HTLC transactions, via a new
AuxSigner.HtlcSigHashType hook.

Add a ResolveHtlcSigHashType helper that queries the aux signer for a
channel-specific sighash override based on negotiated features, falling
back to the default HtlcSigHashType when no aux signer is present or
the feature isn't negotiated. Thread the auxSigner through all HTLC
second-level transaction signing and validation call sites.

Which source the answer comes from follows one rule. The party that
signs a commitment decides its sighash type, from the live feature
negotiation at that time, and a chain whose latest commitment uses
SigHashDefault never goes back. The channel resolves the live answer
when it is constructed and again once the link has re-established the
channel, which is when the aux signer learns the negotiated features
(RefreshHtlcSigHashType). Estimates about future commitments follow the
same answer. A decision about a commitment that already exists, such as
resolving a force close, reads the sighash recorded in the custom blob
of that very commitment.

The receiver of a commitment does not derive its type, it is told. A
commitment_signed is retransmitted as it was first signed, possibly in
a later connection with different features negotiated: one that was
signed before both peers upgraded reaches the receiver after it picked
up the new negotiation, and verifying it as SigHashDefault fails and
force closes the channel. So a commitment_signed that uses
SigHashDefault states it in a custom record, and one without the record
uses the standard sighash flags of the channel type, which is what
every message signed before the feature existed looks like. The
receiver builds and verifies the commitment with the stated type and
refuses SigHashDefault when the feature is not negotiated, a return to
the legacy sighash after its latest commitment used SigHashDefault, and
an unknown value. The type is handed to the aux leaf store with every
commitment that is built (CommitDiffAuxInput.SigHashDefault), so the
blob records what the signer decided rather than what the leaf store
would derive on its own. Only channels with a tapscript root and an aux
signer carry or read the record, the commitment_signed of every other
channel is unchanged.

A channel opened before both peers upgraded therefore switches over
cleanly, also with a commitment_signed in flight: its existing
commitments stay what they were built as, and only new ones use the
negotiated type.

An earlier draft of this feature selected the sighash based on the
presence of the commitment's custom blob alone, which is backwards
incompatible: a peer that has not upgraded would disagree on the
sighash and force close the channel. Explicit feature negotiation
ensures both channel parties agree on the sighash type before it is
ever used.

commit.message:
lnd: don't fail startup if an addpeer peer is already connected

The listener accepts inbound connections before the addpeer loop in
server.Start runs. If a peer listed via addpeer connects to us first,
ConnectToPeer returns errPeerAlreadyConnected and the whole startup is
aborted, even though being connected to the peer is exactly what the
option asks for.

We move the loop into connectToConfigPeers and treat an existing
connection as success. All other errors remain fatal.

Fixes #11582.
